# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On purchasing properties:**
When I land on an unowned property, I buy it if I have the cash available. Properties generate rent income and contribute to my final score, so early acquisition builds my portfolio. Don't overthink it—if I can afford it, I should own it.

**On affording purchases:**
When I cannot afford a property outright, I decline without hesitation. Negative cash is not an option. If I'm stretched thin on cash, I need to reassess whether I'm collecting rent efficiently from my existing deeds.

**On paying rent:**
When I land on an opponent's property, I pay the rent owed immediately and accurately. Track my cash carefully: last declared balance + any transfers received - rent owed = new balance. Don't make arithmetic errors here.

**On passing START:**
When I pass START, I collect my salary. This is free cash—always account for it in my balance update. Every pass is money I should be adding to my reserves.

**On properties I own:**
When I land on a property I own, nothing happens. I owe no rent and cannot buy it again. Move on.

**On strategy going forward:**
I ended with only one property (Quarry) while opponents 1 and 2 each held multiple deeds. This cost me the game. I need to be more aggressive about buying properties early, especially when I have good cash flow. Don't let opponents monopolize the board while I sit on reserves. Every property I pass up is cash my opponents will collect from me later.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On each turn, calculate my true cash position first.** Declare what I paid this turn and what I now hold, keeping my own careful books. The scoring uses my declared balance plus my deed values, so accuracy matters.

**When I land on an unowned property, evaluate it against my current cash and my position in the game.** If I can afford it and it's early enough that I need to build a portfolio, buy it. If I'm running low on cash or late in the game, preserve liquidity—I can't earn rent if I'm broke.

**When I land on someone else's property, pay the rent immediately without hesitation.** This is inevitable and expected; don't waste mental energy on it.

**Recognize that early property acquisition is valuable.** In my last game, I bought Terrace in lap 3 and held it through to the end. This deed contributed to my final score. I should be more aggressive about buying properties early when I have reasonable cash, not wait until I'm too poor to buy anything.

**When I have borderline cash for a property purchase, do the math carefully.** I passed on Exchange for 120 when I had 100—correct decision given the amount. But I should have bought more properties earlier when I had better cash positions.

**At START, always collect my salary.** This is free money each lap; treat it as part of my usable balance.

**Track what other investors own.** Investor 2 accumulated Foundry, Depot, and Wharf. This tells me which properties are still available and which investors are building monopolies. Avoid landing on repeatedly expensive properties; if possible, secure my own properties to avoid this drain.

**By the final lap, I'll have limited options.** Focus on paying what's owed and documenting my final balance accurately, as the game is essentially decided by then.

# Playbook for ref_estate

## Property Acquisition Strategy

When you land on an unowned property, buy it if you have sufficient cash and it generates reasonable rent relative to its cost. Properties with rent-to-cost ratios around 20-25% (like Wharf at 80/18 and Foundry at 100/24) are solid early investments.

Buy properties early in the game when you have capital available, as rental income compounds across laps and other players will visit your properties multiple times.

When you cannot afford a property you land on, simply decline and move on—do not overextend your cash reserves trying to force purchases you cannot make.

## Cash Management

Maintain a minimum cash buffer even after purchases. Do not spend your entire balance on property acquisition, as you need reserves for unexpected rent payments and to continue playing effectively.

Track your running balance carefully: account for salary collected when passing START, all rent received from other players, and all rent you owe when landing on opponents' properties.

## Late-Game Decisions

In the final laps, continue acquiring unowned properties when cash permits. Even properties with lower rent (like Depot at 50/10) become valuable in endgame because other players will land on them during the final lap(s), generating immediate revenue.

Prioritize maintaining positive cash flow and owning multiple properties over hoarding cash, since your final score is cash plus the purchase price of all deeds you hold.
